linger:Café Aliança.name: Café Aliança
linger:Café Aliança.teaser: A café open since 1908 on the marina square, where Faro argued politics and wrote poetry
linger:Café Aliança.story: Aliança opened in 1908 by the marina, and the press still calls it one of the oldest cafés in Portugal (Postal says third oldest). Inside: a revolving door, dark wood panelling, copper over the counter, and on the walls the faces that sat here, Simone de Beauvoir among them, and the Algarve poet António Aleixo. Faro's mayor called it the room where people talked politics and art and wrote poetry and prose. It has closed and reopened several times since 2009; the CTT put it on a stamp in 2017, and it reopened in October 2023 under new management as café, restaurant and bar.
linger:Café Aliança.why: Take a coffee at the counter under the old photographs, then walk out onto the square facing the boats.
facts: Rua Dom Francisco Gomes 7, on the square by the marina
Tuesday to Friday 12:00 to midnight at the 2023 reopening, other hours at weekends (Sul Informação); a visitor blog says it was open again in September 2026 after another closure: check before going
A bica and a pastry at the counter, or a cold beer, as the old cervejaria served
Half an hour with a coffee; a room for looking, not a laptop

linger:Pastelaria Gardy.name: Pastelaria Gardy
linger:Pastelaria Gardy.teaser: Faro's pastry counter since 1953, halfway down the shopping street, for almond, fig and Dom Rodrigo
linger:Pastelaria Gardy.story: Gardy has stood on Rua de Santo António, the white-paved shopping street of the Baixa, since 1953. You come in under brick arches to long glass counters: custard tarts, the little almond and fig sweets of the Algarve, carob cakes, the layered folhados of Tavira and Dom Rodrigo in its twist of foil. Locals stand at the bar for a bica and a pastel de nata; outside, shoppers take a table and a fresh Algarve orange juice. It is a place for the regional sweets in one stop, not a quiet room.
linger:Pastelaria Gardy.why: Buy a box of almond sweets and a Dom Rodrigo here to take back to the boat.
facts: Rua de Santo António 16, in the pedestrian Baixa
Monday to Saturday 08:30 to 19:30, closed Sunday (seen May 2026; not re-checked)

linger:Jardim Manuel Bívar.name: Jardim Manuel Bívar
linger:Jardim Manuel Bívar.teaser: Palms, a bandstand and benches looking west over the marina to the lagoon
linger:Jardim Manuel Bívar.story: The garden fills the strip of land between the Baixa and the little marina, with the walls of the Cidade Velha and the Arco da Vila at its southern end. It is a 19th-century public garden: tall palms, shaded benches and, at its heart, the iron bandstand that the city restored in 2023 as an emblem of the lower town. The tour boats for the islands load at the quay a few steps away. Toward evening the light drops behind the lagoon and the marshes of the Ria Formosa turn copper.
linger:Jardim Manuel Bívar.why: Take a bench facing west in the last hour before sunset: it costs nothing and you see the whole lagoon change colour.
facts: Between the marina, Praça Dom Francisco Gomes and the Arco da Vila
The hour before sunset, on a west-facing bench
Twenty minutes, or a long sit

drink:Negra Mole.name: Negra Mole
drink:Negra Mole.teaser: An old grape with pink, red and black berries on one bunch, poured pale, almost as a rosé
drink:Negra Mole.story: Negra Mole is the grape the Algarve kept. The regional wine commission calls it the second-oldest Portuguese variety after Sercial, and its bunches ripen unevenly, pink, red and near-black berries side by side. That gives a pale, low-tannin wine of fresh red fruit, the old palhete and clarete of Algarve tables. In the late 20th century it disappeared into anonymous blends, and many vineyards were pulled up for resorts and golf. From about 2010 growers began bottling it alone again, now as light reds, rosés and traditional-method sparklers: Cabrita in Silves makes a blanc de noirs and a rosé from it, Morgado do Quintão an espumante.
drink:Negra Mole.why: Ask for it slightly cool with grilled fish: it is the red that does not fight the sea.
facts: Pale ruby, red cherry and strawberry, light tannin; sparkling versions are white or pale pink
Negra Mole; DOP Lagoa, Portimão, Lagos or Tavira, or Vinho Regional Algarve; palhete or clarete for the light old style
Cabrita's Negra Mole blanc de noirs or rosé sparkling; Morgado do Quintão's espumante or clarete. A bottle at about EUR 12 to 30 (seen May 2026)

drink:Arinto.name: Arinto
drink:Arinto.teaser: The white that stays sharp in the southern heat: lemon, green apple, a mineral finish
drink:Arinto.story: Arinto is grown all over Portugal for one reason: it holds its acidity when the sun does its worst. In the Algarve it is the backbone of most serious white blends and is also bottled alone. Young, it tastes of lemon, lime and green apple with a stony finish; some producers ferment or age it in barrel, which rounds it without losing the edge. That bite is what you want against a cataplana or a plate of clams, where butter, oil and lagoon brine need something to cut them.
drink:Arinto.why: The safe white order at any Algarve table where shellfish is coming.
facts: Pale lemon, citrus and green apple, high acidity, a mineral finish
Arinto, alone or first in a blend with Crato Branco or other whites
A young Algarve Arinto with shellfish; a barrel-aged one with richer fish. About EUR 10 to 25 a bottle (seen May 2026)

drink:Crato Branco.name: Crato Branco
drink:Crato Branco.teaser: The Algarve's own name for Síria, a softer, more aromatic white than Arinto
drink:Crato Branco.story: Order Crato Branco in Faro and you are drinking a grape that changes its name at every provincial border: Síria is its official Portuguese name, Roupeiro in the Alentejo, Códega in the Douro, Crato Branco here. It ripens late and gives a fragrant white, ripe stone fruit and flowers, rounder and softer than Arinto, so the two are often blended. Its history in the Algarve is long: José André Cabrita planted it at Quinta da Vinha, near Silves, in 1977, and Morgado do Quintão bottles it on its own.
drink:Crato Branco.why: Drink it with grilled fish or a sea bream baked in salt, where Arinto would be too sharp.
facts: Pale gold, peach, melon and flowers, softer acidity than Arinto
Crato Branco, sometimes Síria or Roupeiro; often blended with Arinto
Morgado do Quintão's single-variety Crato Branco, or Cabrita's whites from Silves. About EUR 14 to 25 a bottle (seen May 2026)

drink:Medronho.name: Medronho
drink:Medronho.teaser: Clear and strong, distilled from the wild red berries of the strawberry tree in the Monchique hills
drink:Medronho.story: The strawberry tree, medronheiro, grows wild on the schist hills of the Serra de Monchique, and in autumn its round berries turn from yellow to deep red. Families pick them, leave them to ferment for weeks, about two months for one Monchique maker, then distil the mash in copper stills over the winter, often into February and March. The result is clear, very strong and smells of ripe fruit and the hillside; aged in wood, it turns gold. The old guide, citing DGADR, gives it a protected name, Medronho do Algarve IGP; the regional wine commission was named its certifier in 2016. The still itself: see Casa do Medronho.
drink:Medronho.why: A small glass after coffee, at room temperature, in a tasca that buys from a hill family.
facts: Clear (gold if aged), ripe red fruit and earth; very strong, often close to 50% (the old guide said about 48%)
Aguardente de Medronho; Medronho do Algarve for the protected name; a certified distillery's name
A medronho from Monchique, not chilled, a small pour after coffee. About EUR 12 to 25 a bottle (seen May 2026)

drink:Bagaceira.name: Bagaceira
drink:Bagaceira.teaser: Portugal's grape-skin brandy, the cousin of grappa, poured after a long lunch
drink:Bagaceira.story: When the wine is pressed, the skins, pips and stalks left behind are not wasted: they are distilled into bagaceira, Portugal's answer to marc and grappa. Young, it is clear, hot and grapey; aged in oak as bagaceira velha it turns amber and softer. It is made across the country, and the Algarve has no protected name of its own, but some cellars distil the pomace of their own grapes, Negra Mole and Castelão among them. Ask at a winery tasting whether they have one.
drink:Bagaceira.why: Ask for it when medronho is too fierce: same ritual, a grape-skin taste.
facts: Clear and fiery young; amber, softer and woodier when aged
Aguardente bagaceira; velha for oak-aged; at least 37.5% by law
A bagaceira velha after lunch, or a cellar's own at a tasting. About EUR 10 to 30 a bottle (seen May 2026)

bars:Bago Wine Bar.name: Bago Wine Bar
bars:Bago Wine Bar.teaser: A small Baixa wine bar run by Rui Martins, with Portuguese and natural wines open by the glass
bars:Bago Wine Bar.story: Bago is on a quiet side street in the Baixa, with a few tables on the terrace and shelves of bottles inside. Its owner, Rui Martins, buys Portuguese wine, much of it natural, organic or biodynamic, and keeps about ten bottles open to pour by the glass, so you can taste an Algarve Negra Mole beside something from the Douro or Bairrada. Small plates come with it: cheese, charcuterie, toasts, roast black-pork sausage. It is listed on Raisin, the natural-wine guide, and on Friday evenings there has often been live music.
bars:Bago Wine Bar.why: Let them pour you a flight of the Algarve list before dinner.
facts: About ten wines open by the glass, Portuguese and natural; Algarve Negra Mole and Crato Branco on the list
About EUR 5 to 12 a glass, plates EUR 8 to 18 (seen May 2026)
Early evening; Tuesday to Saturday 10:00 to 23:00, Sunday 10:00 to 15:00, closed Monday (Raisin listing, Oct 2026); winter break in January in past years

bars:The Hotel Faro rooftop.name: Cosmopolitan, Hotel Faro rooftop
bars:The Hotel Faro rooftop.teaser: Fifth-floor cocktails over the marina, facing west across the lagoon
bars:The Hotel Faro rooftop.story: The Cosmopolitan bar sits on the fifth-floor roof of Hotel Faro, on the square at the head of the marina. It faces west, so from the terrace you look over the masts and the Jardim Manuel Bívar to the marshes of the Ria Formosa and the line of the barrier islands. The cocktails are named after airlines; the crowd is hotel guests and visitors in for the view, and the music is occasional. It is not a bargain, and the view is what you are paying for.
bars:The Hotel Faro rooftop.why: Go up for one drink as the sun goes down over the lagoon, then walk on to dinner.
facts: Hotel Faro, Praça Dom Francisco Gomes 2, fifth floor
Signature cocktails named after airlines, classic cocktails, wine and beer
About EUR 8 to 15 a drink (seen May 2026)
